docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This guide helps Java developers familiar with Spring understand GraphQL and build GraphQL APIs with Spring GraphQL and the Netflix DGS framework. It starts with the GraphQL specification and its transport protocols, then covers GraphQL Java — the execution engine that every JVM framework builds on — and finishes with the two Spring-based frameworks, their history, and their relationship.

The examples use Java 25 and Spring Boot 4.1.2 / Spring Framework 7. Some examples are written in Kotlin (Kotlin 2.4.x). This guide is not a Spring tutorial; it assumes you can already build a Spring Boot application.

docs.title: Get the examples
docs.text:
The spring-graphql-sample repository contains the example projects. Clone it with Git:

git clone https://github.com/hantsy/spring-graphql-sample.git

Each example is a standalone Maven project with its own Maven Wrapper. See the README for the full example index and build instructions.

docs.title: Read this guide
docs.text: If you are new to GraphQL on the JVM, read An introduction to GraphQL and Spring: what GraphQL is and why you would use it instead of REST, the schema language and the request/response protocol, the HTTP and WebSocket transports, the GraphQL Java execution engine, and the Netflix DGS and Spring GraphQL frameworks.

docs.title: An introduction to GraphQL and Spring
docs.text:
GraphQL is more and more popular in developer communities. What began as an internal Facebook tool for mobile apps is now a cross-ecosystem standard, with servers and tooling for nearly every language and platform. On the JVM, that means one shared engine — GraphQL Java — and two Spring Boot frameworks built on top of it.

This chapter is for Java developers who know Spring and want to understand GraphQL and the frameworks that run it on the JVM. The examples use Java 25 and Spring Boot 4.1.2 / Spring Framework 7, with some written in Kotlin (Kotlin 2.4.x). This chapter is not a Spring tutorial; it assumes you can already build a Spring Boot application.

docs.title: What is GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL is a query language for APIs and a runtime for executing those queries against your data. Facebook's mobile apps have been powered by GraphQL since 2012. The specification was open-sourced in 2015 and is now maintained by the GraphQL Foundation, hosted by the Linux Foundation since 2018.

A GraphQL server exposes a single endpoint and a strongly typed schema. The client sends a document that describes exactly the data it needs, and the server responds with JSON in the same shape. Compared with a REST API, this moves the choice of response shape from the server to the client.

The specification defines three kinds of operations:

  • Query — read data.
  • Mutation — write data, executed serially in the order the document lists them.
  • Subscription — a long-lived operation that pushes a stream of results to the client as events happen.

The specification deliberately says nothing about the transport. HTTP and WebSocket are the common choices, and separate specifications cover them.

docs.title: The REST problem
docs.text:
Consider a blog screen that shows a post, its author, and the latest three comments. Against a typical REST API, that one screen takes several calls:

  • GET /posts/1 returns the whole post — id, title, content, tags, and timestamps — even though the screen only needs the title.
  • GET /posts/1/comments returns every comment, so the client filters the latest three itself.
  • GET /authors/7 returns the full author profile just to show one name.

The client over-fetches fields it does not use, under-fetches data it must assemble from several endpoints, and pays a round trip for each call. The usual fix is a bespoke endpoint such as GET /posts/1?include=author,comments — and then one of those per screen. REST's resource-per-URL model works well for simple, independent resources, but it fights you as soon as the data forms a graph.

docs.title: The GraphQL approach
docs.text:
GraphQL turns the request around. The client describes the graph it needs in a single document, and the server resolves it in one round trip:

{
  postById(postId: "1") {
    title
    author { name }
    comments { content }
  }
}

The response comes back in the same shape, which removes the REST problems:

  • No over-fetching. The query asks for exactly the fields it needs — the post's title, not its tags or timestamps.
  • No under-fetching, no round trips. The author and the comments ride along in the same response.
  • A typed, introspectable contract. The schema is machine-readable, so tools generate clients, validate queries, and offer autocomplete (GraphiQL, Apollo Client) without a separate API-description layer such as OpenAPI.
  • One endpoint, no versioning. GraphQL has no per-resource URLs. Adding a field is additive and does not break existing clients.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
GraphQL is not a free lunch. The costs sit mostly on the server:

  • Harder caching. GraphQL responses are not addressed by URL, so HTTP caching does not apply as naturally as it does to REST resources.
  • Query cost on the server. The server must parse, validate, and bound every query, so a deep or expensive query is a real operational concern.
  • No built-in file upload. Uploads need the separate multipart request specification.
  • More moving parts. A GraphQL server and its toolchain are more to build and operate than a simple REST endpoint.

REST remains the simpler fit for small, resource-oriented, cacheable APIs. GraphQL pays off when clients are many, diverse, and evolve independently of the server.

docs.title: Schema and SDL
docs.text:
A GraphQL schema is a contract written in the Schema Definition Language (SDL). It declares the types a server exposes and the operations clients can run. The following schema is the one used by the dgs example (comments and formatting trimmed):

type Post {
    id: ID!
    title: String!
    content: String
    comments: [Comment]
    authorId: String
    author: Author
}

type Author {
    id: ID!
    name: String!
    email: String!
    posts: [Post]
}

type Comment {
    id: ID!
    content: String!
    postId: String!
}

input CreatePostInput {
    title: String!
    content: String!
}

type Query {
    allPosts: [Post!]!
    postById(postId: ID!): Post
}

type Mutation {
    createPost(createPostInput: CreatePostInput!): Post!
}

The building blocks are:

  • Object types (type Post) — named collections of fields. Each field has a type and can take arguments, such as postById(postId: ID!).
  • Scalar types — the leaf values. The built-in scalars are Int, Float, String, Boolean, and ID. Servers can add custom scalars such as Date or Upload.
  • Input types (input CreatePostInput) — structured arguments for mutations. Only input types, scalars, and enums can be used as input.
  • Enums — a fixed set of named values, for example enum PostStatus { DRAFT PUBLISHED }.
  • Interfaces and unions — abstract types that let a field return one of several object types. A type resolver picks the concrete type at runtime.
  • Non-null (!) and lists ([]) — modifiers. Post! never returns null, [Post!]! is a non-null list of non-null posts, and [Post] can be null and can contain nulls.
  • Directives — annotations such as @deprecated(reason: "...") that change how the schema or a document executes. Servers can define custom directives.

Three root types anchor every schema:

  • Query — the entry point for reads.
  • Mutation — the entry point for writes. Top-level mutation fields execute serially, in document order; query fields can execute in parallel.
  • Subscription — the entry point for event streams. A subscription field returns a stream of results rather than a single value.

The names are conventions; a schema declaration can rename them, but most servers — and every example in this repository — use the defaults.

A schema is also queryable. Clients ask the server for its own types through the meta-fields __schema and __type, which is how tools such as GraphiQL provide completion and documentation:

{
  __schema {
    types {
      name
    }
  }
}

Introspection is part of the specification, so it works against any compliant server. The specification is published in dated editions (June 2018, October 2021, September 2025), with a draft of the next edition always available.

docs.title: GraphQL request lifecycle
docs.text: A GraphQL request follows the same lifecycle on every transport: the client sends a document, the server parses and validates it against the schema, executes the operation, and returns a response. The next two sections walk through the request and the response.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
A GraphQL request carries three members:

  • query — the document: one or more operations, each a query, mutation, or subscription.
  • variables — a JSON object of values for the variables the document declares. Optional.
  • operationName — which operation to run when the document contains more than one. Optional.

Over HTTP, the client POSTs this as a JSON body. The following request reads every post with its title and author name:

curl http://localhost:8080/graphql \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "{ allPosts { id title author { name } } }"}'

Never build a document by concatenating user input into the query string. Declare variables instead, and let the server coerce and validate them:

curl http://localhost:8080/graphql \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": "query PostById($postId: ID!) { postById(postId: $postId) { title content } }",
    "variables": { "postId": "1" },
    "operationName": "PostById"
  }'

The document declares $postId: ID!; the variables object supplies the value. The server validates the document against the schema before any data fetcher runs. A mutation uses the same envelope:

curl http://localhost:8080/graphql \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "query": "mutation CreatePost($input: CreatePostInput!) { createPost(createPostInput: $input) { id title } }",
    "variables": { "input": { "title": "Hello GraphQL", "content": "First post" } }
  }'

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
A GraphQL response is a JSON object with up to three members:

  • data — the result, in the same shape as the operation's selection set.
  • errors — a list of errors raised while validating or executing the operation. Present only when something went wrong.
  • extensions — an optional map for server-specific additions, such as tracing data.

A successful response to the allPosts query looks like this:

{
  "data": {
    "allPosts": [
      { "id": "1", "title": "Hello GraphQL", "author": { "name": "Hantsy" } }
    ]
  }
}

GraphQL distinguishes request errors from field errors. A request error — a syntax error, a validation failure, an unknown operation — rejects the whole operation, and the response has errors and no data. A field error — a data fetcher that throws — nulls out only that field, and the rest of the response still returns:

{
  "data": {
    "postById": {
      "title": "Hello GraphQL",
      "author": null
    }
  },
  "errors": [
    {
      "message": "Failed to load author",
      "locations": [{ "line": 1, "column": 40 }],
      "path": ["postById", "author"]
    }
  ]
}

Each error carries a message, the locations in the document that caused it, and the path to the field that failed. If a non-null field (Author!) errors, the null propagates up to the nearest nullable parent — the schema's nullability rules decide how much of the response survives.

docs.title: Runtime protocols
docs.text: The GraphQL specification does not define a transport. Two conventions cover the real world: HTTP for queries and mutations, and WebSocket (or Server-Sent Events) for subscriptions.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
The GraphQL over HTTP specification formalizes how GraphQL runs over HTTP. A server must support GraphQL requests via POST with a UTF-8 JSON body and the Content-Type: application/json header. Every example in this repository accepts POST on /graphql. A server may also support GET for read-only queries, with the request members moved into the URL query string; GET must not execute mutations (the recommended response is 405 Method Not Allowed). GET is useful for caching but optional — do not rely on it being enabled.

Two media types matter. application/json is the legacy request and response type. application/graphql-response+json is the newer response type, sent in the Accept header, typically as application/graphql-response+json, application/json;q=0.9 so older servers can fall back. The media type decides how errors map to HTTP status codes: with application/graphql-response+json, a request-level error produces a 4xx or 5xx, while a well-formed operation that executes — even with field errors — produces 2xx. With legacy application/json, most servers return 200 OK for any well-formed response and signal problems only in the errors member. A GraphQL client must always inspect the response body: a 200 status does not mean every field succeeded.

docs.title: Subscriptions over SSE
docs.text: Subscriptions need a channel that stays open. Over plain HTTP, the client POSTs the subscription document with Accept: text/event-stream, and the server keeps the response open and writes one data: event per result. The GraphQL over Server-Sent Events protocol defines these events. The -http modules — for example spring-graphql-webmvc-http — serve queries, mutations, and SSE subscriptions on the same /graphql endpoint.

docs.title: Subscriptions over WebSocket
docs.text:
A subscription over WebSocket uses a subprotocol, and two exist that are not compatible with each other. The first, subscriptions-transport-ws (Apollo, 2016), is no longer maintained. The actively maintained replacement is graphql-ws, whose GraphQL over WebSocket Protocol uses the subprotocol graphql-transport-ws and lets any operation — query, mutation, or subscription — run over the socket:

Message Direction Purpose ConnectionInit / ConnectionAck client ↔ server Open the connection; operations are allowed only after the ack. Subscribe client → server Start an operation under a unique id. Next server → client One execution result from the operation's stream. Error server → client Execution errors for the operation; the stream finishes. Complete either The stream finishes; the client can also send it to unsubscribe. Ping / Pong either Bidirectional heartbeat.

Because the protocols are distinct, migrating means upgrading the client and the server together — a graphql-ws client cannot talk to a subscriptions-transport-ws server. The WebSocket examples in this repository all speak graphql-transport-ws.

docs.title: File upload
docs.text: The specification does not define file uploads. The interoperable standard is the GraphQL multipart request specification, which wraps the usual operations JSON in a multipart form and maps file fields to object paths. For Spring GraphQL and DGS support, see How DGS adopted Spring GraphQL.

docs.title: GraphQL Java
docs.text: GraphQL Java is the JVM implementation of the GraphQL specification, started in 2015. It is an execution engine, not a server framework: it parses schemas, validates documents, and executes operations, but it knows nothing about HTTP, WebSocket, or Spring. Every framework in this repository — Spring GraphQL, Netflix DGS, and the legacy Kickstart and SPQR examples — embeds it and delegates execution to it.

docs.title: Build the schema
docs.text:
Execution starts with a GraphQLSchema. The schema-first path parses SDL into a TypeDefinitionRegistry, then combines it with a RuntimeWiring to produce an executable schema:

TypeDefinitionRegistry typeRegistry =
        new SchemaParser().parse(new ClassPathResource("/schema/schema.graphql").getFile());

GraphQLSchema graphQLSchema =
        new SchemaGenerator().makeExecutableSchema(typeRegistry, runtimeWiring);

RuntimeWiring is where behavior attaches to the type system: data fetchers, custom scalars, directives, and type resolvers for interfaces and unions:

RuntimeWiring.newRuntimeWiring()
        .codeRegistry(codeRegistry)
        .scalar(Scalars.localDateTimeType())
        .scalar(Scalars.uuidType())
        .directive("uppercase", new UpperCaseDirectiveWiring())
        .build();

A code-first path also exists — building GraphQLSchema programmatically with builders instead of SDL — but every example in this repository is schema-first.

docs.title: Fetch data
docs.text:
A DataFetcher<T> resolves one field. It receives a DataFetchingEnvironment with the field arguments, the parent object, the execution context, and the data loader registry:

public DataFetcher<Post> postById() {
    return (DataFetchingEnvironment dfe) -> {
        String postId = dfe.getArgument("postId");
        return postService.getPostById(postId);
    };
}

Fields without an explicit fetcher fall back to PropertyDataFetcher, which reads a matching property from the parent object — this is why a Post record with a title accessor needs no wiring for its title field. A fetcher can return a plain value, a CompletionStage for asynchronous work, or a reactive Publisher for subscription fields.

docs.title: Execute operations
docs.text:
The GraphQL object is the engine entry point. Build it once from the schema, then execute an ExecutionInput per request:

GraphQL graphQL = GraphQL.newGraphQL(graphQLSchema).build();

ExecutionInput input = ExecutionInput.newExecutionInput()
        .query("{ allPosts { id title } }")
        .build();

ExecutionResult result = graphQL.execute(input);
Map<String, Object> data = result.getData();
List<GraphQLError> errors = result.getErrors();

executeAsync returns a CompletableFuture<ExecutionResult> instead. The ExecutionResult maps directly to the response envelope. The engine picks an execution strategy per operation type: query fields resolve in parallel, mutation fields resolve serially in document order, and subscription fields resolve to a stream that the transport layer forwards to the client.

docs.title: Batch with DataLoader
docs.text:
Naive field resolution produces the N+1 problem: loading ten posts and then each post's comments runs eleven queries. The java-dataloader library — a separate project under the GraphQL Java organization — batches and caches loads per request. Before, one query per post:

SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id = ?
SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id = ?
SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id = ?

After, one batched query:

SELECT * FROM comments WHERE post_id in (?, ?, ?, ?)

A fetcher asks the environment for a registered loader and loads a key; the loader collects keys during the execution tick and dispatches them as one batch:

DataLoader<String, Author> dataLoader = dfe.getDataLoader("authorsLoader");
return dataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());

Loaders are registered in a DataLoaderRegistry keyed by name. Spring GraphQL and DGS both build on this same mechanism.

docs.title: GraphQL in the Java ecosystem
docs.text:
GraphQL on the JVM has gone through several generations of integration libraries. GraphQL Java is the low-level engine; Netflix DGS and Spring GraphQL are the two actively maintained Spring Boot frameworks built on top of it. The framework links come from the README.

  • 2015: GraphQL Java. Facebook open-sourced the specification, and GraphQL Java started the same year as the JVM implementation — schema parsing, validation, and execution, but no way to serve requests.
  • 2016: graphql-java-servlet. A servlet endpoint that accepted GraphQL requests over HTTP and handed them to a GraphQL instance, with an early WebSocket subscription implementation.
  • The Kickstart era. GraphQL Java Kickstart built the most popular Spring Boot integration of that period on GraphQL Java Tools (schema-first resolver wiring) and the GraphQL Spring Boot Starters (auto-configuration for the servlet, GraphiQL, and subscriptions). The starters are now archived: "Since Spring now officially supports GraphQL we have decided to archive this project."
  • The code-first alternative: SPQR. GraphQL SPQR annotated plain Java methods and generated the schema from the code. Development is no longer active, but the code-first approach lives on in MicroProfile GraphQL, implemented by SmallRye GraphQL and supported in Quarkus.
  • 2021: Netflix DGS. Netflix open-sourced the DGS (Domain Graph Service) framework in February 2021 after years of internal use — an annotation-based Spring Boot programming model, schema code generation, federation support, and a query-test framework.
  • 2021–2022: Spring GraphQL. The Spring team built Spring GraphQL directly on GraphQL Java. Version 1.0 arrived in May 2022, and Spring Boot 2.7 shipped spring-boot-starter-graphql — GraphQL became an official part of the Spring portfolio.

The ecosystem today:

Project Approach Status GraphQL Java Execution engine Active; the foundation of everything below. Spring GraphQL Official Spring integration, schema-first controllers Active; the Spring baseline. Netflix DGS Annotation model, codegen, federation, on Spring GraphQL Active. GraphQL Kotlin Code-first Kotlin, coroutines (ExpediaGroup) Active. GraphQL Java Kickstart Schema-first tools + Spring Boot starters Starters archived; use Spring GraphQL. GraphQL SPQR Code-first schema generation Inactive.

Outside Spring, the author's companion repositories show GraphQL Java with Quarkus and Vert.x. The legacy/ folder in this repository preserves the discontinued stacks — Kickstart, SPQR, vanilla GraphQL Java — on the Spring Boot and Java versions they were last verified with; the active modules track current Spring Boot and either Spring GraphQL or DGS.

docs.title: Netflix DGS and Spring GraphQL
docs.text: Two Spring Boot frameworks dominate GraphQL on the JVM today, and since 2024 they are no longer competitors at the engine level: the Netflix DGS framework is built on Spring GraphQL.

docs.title: Netflix DGS
docs.text:
The DGS (Domain Graph Service) framework is Netflix's GraphQL server framework for Spring Boot, open-sourced in 2021. It is schema-first: you write SDL under src/main/resources/schema/, then implement data fetchers as annotated Spring components:

@DgsComponent
public class PostsDataFetcher {
    private final PostService postService;

    @DgsQuery
    public List<Post> allPosts() {
        return this.postService.getAllPosts();
    }

    @DgsQuery
    public Post postById(@InputArgument Long postId) {
        return this.postService.getPostById(postId);
    }

    @DgsData(parentType = "Post", field = "author")
    public CompletableFuture<Author> author(DgsDataFetchingEnvironment dfe) {
        DataLoader<Long, Author> dataLoader = dfe.getDataLoader("authorsLoader");
        Post post = dfe.getSource();
        return dataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());
    }

    @DgsMutation
    public Post createPost(@InputArgument("createPostInput") CreatePostInput input) {
        var id = this.postService.createPost(input);
        return this.postService.getPostById(id);
    }
}

The annotations map directly to the schema: @DgsComponent marks the class as a data fetcher container, @DgsQuery / @DgsMutation / @DgsSubscription bind a method to a root-type field, @DgsData(parentType = "...", field = "...") binds a method to any field on any type, and @InputArgument binds a GraphQL argument to a method parameter. Subscriptions return a reactive Publisher.

Note

The DGS framework itself is written mainly in Kotlin. This is an implementation detail — DGS works equally well from Java, and this repository demonstrates both the Java (dgs) and Kotlin (dgs-kotlin, dgs-kotlin-co) styles.

DGS also ships a codegen plugin that generates Java or Kotlin types from the schema (the dgs-codegen example), first-class Apollo Federation support for federated subgraphs, and a test framework (DgsQueryExecutor, @DgsTest).

docs.title: Spring GraphQL
docs.text:
Spring GraphQL is the Spring team's official GraphQL support, built on GraphQL Java. Version 1.0 arrived in May 2022, and Spring Boot 2.7 introduced spring-boot-starter-graphql. It is also schema-first, with SDL files under src/main/resources/graphql/ and annotated controllers in the style of Spring MVC:

@Controller
public class PostController {
    private final PostService postService;

    @QueryMapping
    public List<Post> allPosts() {
        return this.postService.getAllPosts();
    }

    @QueryMapping
    public Post postById(@Argument("postId") String id) {
        return this.postService.getPostById(id);
    }

    @MutationMapping
    public Post createPost(@Argument("createPostInput") @Valid CreatePostInput input) {
        return postService.createPost(input);
    }

    @SubscriptionMapping
    public Publisher<Comment> commentAdded() {
        return this.postService.commentAdded();
    }

    @SchemaMapping(field = "author")
    public CompletionStage<Author> authorOfPost(
            Post post, DataLoader<String, Author> authorDataLoader) {
        return authorDataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());
    }
}

@QueryMapping, @MutationMapping, and @SubscriptionMapping bind a method to a root-type field; @SchemaMapping binds a method to a field on any type; @Argument binds a GraphQL argument with coercion and Bean Validation (@Valid) support. Methods can return plain values, CompletionStage, or reactive types.

Spring GraphQL separates execution from transport, so the same application code runs on WebMvc, WebFlux, WebSocket, and RSocket. It wraps GraphQL Java's DataLoader mechanism in a BatchLoaderRegistry, ships a dedicated testing API (@GraphQlTest slices with a protocol-neutral GraphQlTester, plus HttpGraphQlTester and WebSocketGraphQlTester), and provides the production client API (HttpSyncGraphQlClient, HttpGraphQlClient, WebSocketGraphQlClient).

docs.title: How DGS adopted Spring GraphQL
docs.text:
Netflix open-sourced DGS in 2021 and it became the most widely adopted GraphQL Java framework. Soon after, the DGS team learned of a parallel effort by the Spring team — Spring for GraphQL — and over the following year Spring GraphQL matured to rough feature parity with DGS. The result was two frameworks solving the same problem: new users had to choose, the maintainers duplicated work, and the community's feedback split across two projects.

Neither could simply disappear. DGS is deeply embedded in many companies' architectures (including Netflix's), so forcing a migration would be costly with no benefit; at the same time, Spring deserves an out-of-the-box GraphQL offering. The teams chose integration over competition. DGS keeps its programming model and tooling but drops the parts that duplicated Spring GraphQL's low-level WebMvc/WebFlux integration. The integration shipped first as an opt-in spring-graphql flavor of the DGS starter, then became the default in DGS 9.0 (May 2024), which builds against Spring GraphQL 1.3, Spring Boot 3.3, and GraphQL Java 22. DGS 10.0.0 (December 2024) removed the legacy WebMvc/WebFlux code, making Spring GraphQL the sole foundation.

After the integration:

  • You write data fetchers with the DGS programming model (@DgsComponent, @DgsQuery), the Spring GraphQL programming model (@QueryMapping), or both in the same application.
  • DGS builds the GraphQLSchema from its programming model and schema files.
  • Spring GraphQL handles the transports and executes every operation through its ExecutionGraphQlService.
  • DgsQueryExecutor becomes a proxy over ExecutionGraphQlService, so existing DGS test code keeps working unchanged.

One engine, one transport layer, two programming models. For your code the integration is mostly a drop-in replacement — the areas to review when upgrading are the ones where the frameworks overlapped: configuration properties, file uploads, WebSocket subscriptions, schema inspection, and test setup. See Netflix's Spring GraphQL Integration document for the full list.

The two frameworks now share the same foundation — both run on Spring Boot, both execute with GraphQL Java, and DGS additionally uses Spring GraphQL's execution service and transports. The differences that remain are the programming model and the tooling around it:

Aspect Netflix DGS Spring GraphQL Programming model @DgsComponent classes with @DgsQuery, @DgsData, @InputArgument @Controller classes with @QueryMapping, @SchemaMapping, @Argument Schema location src/main/resources/schema/ src/main/resources/graphql/ Code generation Official Gradle/Maven plugin generates types from the schema No built-in codegen; use a third-party plugin if wanted Federation Built-in subgraph support Not built in; add a federation library Testing DgsQueryExecutor, @DgsTest GraphQlTester, @GraphQlTest, transport testers Client Typesafe client generated from the schema HttpSyncGraphQlClient, HttpGraphQlClient, WebSocketGraphQlClient Transports HTTP, SSE, WebSocket (via Spring GraphQL) HTTP, SSE, WebSocket, RSocket Stewardship Netflix Spring team Dependency management DGS platform BOM aligned to a Boot version Spring Boot starter, version managed by Boot

Both support Kotlin and coroutines, Spring Security, and DataLoader-based batching.

File upload is one concrete difference. Spring GraphQL never implemented the GraphQL multipart request specification, and DGS's built-in file upload left with the legacy code in DGS 10.0.0. To add file upload to a Spring GraphQL or DGS application, use multipart-spring-graphql (name.nkonev.multipart-spring-graphql:multipart-spring-graphql), which maps the Upload scalar to a Spring MultipartFile. The dgs-fileupload example has been updated to use it.

docs.title: GraphQL Kotlin
docs.text:
GraphQL Kotlin is Expedia Group's code-first GraphQL library for Kotlin. Unlike DGS and Spring GraphQL, which are schema-first, GraphQL Kotlin generates the schema from your Kotlin code, so there is no SDL to maintain.

It ships server integrations for both Spring and Ktor, with first-class coroutine support, plus schema generation, federation, and client tooling. The graphql-kotlin example demonstrates it with Spring Boot.

docs.title: Choosing a framework
docs.text:
• Starting a new Spring Boot application — choose Spring GraphQL. It is the official Spring baseline, its versions move with Spring Boot, and its controller model matches the rest of a Spring application.
  • Running DGS today — stay on DGS and keep upgrading. Since DGS 9 you are already on Spring GraphQL underneath; a rewrite buys nothing, and you can mix Spring GraphQL APIs into a DGS application where they help.
  • Needing codegen or federation — DGS's generated types and built-in federation support are the strongest reasons to pick it for a new project.
  • Preferring code-first Kotlin — look at GraphQL Kotlin instead; it generates the schema from Kotlin code rather than requiring SDL.

The dgs* modules demonstrate the DGS programming model and the spring-graphql* modules demonstrate Spring GraphQL across every transport; both run the same blog domain (posts, authors, comments) against the same Postgres schema, so you can compare equivalent implementations directly.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
You have seen what GraphQL is and why you would choose it over REST, the schema language (SDL) and the request lifecycle, the HTTP and WebSocket transports, and the GraphQL Java execution engine. You have also met the two Spring Boot frameworks — Netflix DGS and Spring GraphQL — how DGS adopted Spring GraphQL as its foundation, and how to choose between them.

To go further, clone the spring-graphql-sample repository and run one of the dgs* or spring-graphql* modules.

docs.title: Getting started with Netflix DGS
docs.text:
Netflix DGS (Domain Graph Service) is the GraphQL server framework that Netflix open-sourced in 2021 and has run in production since. It gives Spring Boot developers a schema-first, annotation-driven way to build GraphQL APIs on top of GraphQL Java.

In this guide you build a small blog API — Post, Author, and Comment — and, along the way, meet the pieces that make up a DGS application: the schema, data fetchers, data loaders, error handling, and validation. From there you extend it to a reactive WebFlux stack, generate types with the DGS codegen plugin, call the API with the generated client, and accept file uploads.

Every section maps to a working module in the spring-graphql-sample repository. The code excerpts are trimmed to the parts that matter.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Java 25 — the examples target Spring Boot 4.1.2 / Spring Framework 7.
  • Docker — the blog API stores data in PostgreSQL, started with Docker Compose.
  • Maven — optional; every module ships its own Maven Wrapper (mvnw).

docs.title: The blog domain and schema
docs.text:
DGS is schema-first: you describe the API in the GraphQL Schema Definition Language (SDL), and DGS wires your Java code to it. The dgs module declares the following schema in src/main/resources/schema/schema.graphql:

type Post {
    id: ID!
    title: String!
    content: String
    comments: [Comment]
    authorId: String
    author: Author
}

type Author {
    id: ID!
    name: String!
    email: String!
    posts: [Post]
}

type Comment {
    id: ID!
    content: String!
    postId: String!
}

input CreatePostInput {
    title: String!
    content: String!
}

type Query {
    allPosts: [Post!]!
    postById(postId: ID!): Post
}

type Mutation {
    createPost(createPostInput: CreatePostInput!): Post!
}

The three object types are the nodes of the graph, CreatePostInput is the argument you pass to create a post, and the Query and Mutation root types are the entry points clients call.

docs.title: Project setup
docs.text:
The pom.xml brings in the DGS platform BOM so all DGS artifacts stay on one version, then the starter and the usual Spring Boot pieces:

<properties>
    <java.version>25</java.version>
    <dgs-platform.version>12.1.0</dgs-platform.version>
</properties>

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.netflix.graphql.dgs</groupId>
            <artifactId>graphql-dgs-platform-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>${dgs-platform.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.netflix.graphql.dgs</groupId>
        <artifactId>dgs-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jdbc</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
        <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
        <scope>runtime</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
        <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
        <scope>provided</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
  • dgs-starter is the DGS auto-configuration. Since DGS 9 it is built on Spring GraphQL, so it also pulls in Spring GraphQL's execution and transport support.
  • spring-boot-starter-webmvc provides the HTTP endpoint.
  • spring-boot-starter-validation enables Bean Validation on input types.
  • spring-boot-starter-data-jdbc and the PostgreSQL driver give us a JdbcClient for persistence.

The data layer is minimal. schema.sql creates the tables, and spring.sql.init.mode=always in application.properties runs it on startup:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name       VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    email      VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS posts (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    title      VARCHAR(255),
    content    VARCHAR(255),
    status     VARCHAR(255) DEFAULT 'DRAFT',
    author_id  BIGINT REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS comments (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    content    VARCHAR(255),
    post_id    BIGINT REFERENCES posts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

The repository layer is plain Spring JdbcClient. Here is the write path that createPost uses:

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PostRepository {
    private final JdbcClient jdbcClient;

    public Long create(String title, String content, String status, Long authorId) {
        String sql = """
                INSERT INTO posts (title, content, status, author_id)
                VALUES (:title, :content, :status, :author_id)
                """;
        GeneratedKeyHolder keyHolder = new GeneratedKeyHolder();
        this.jdbcClient.sql(sql)
                .param("title", title)
                .param("content", content)
                .param("status", status)
                .param("author_id", authorId)
                .update(keyHolder, "id");
        return keyHolder.getKeyAs(Long.class);
    }
}

docs.title: Data fetchers
docs.text:
Data fetchers are where the schema meets your Java code. You mark a class with @DgsComponent and its methods with the DGS annotations, which bind a method to a schema field by name:

@DgsComponent
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PostsDataFetcher {
    private final PostService postService;

    @DgsQuery
    public List<Post> allPosts() {
        return this.postService.getAllPosts();
    }

    @DgsQuery
    public Post postById(@InputArgument Long postId) {
        return this.postService.getPostById(postId);
    }

    @DgsData(parentType = "Post", field = "author")
    public CompletableFuture<Author> author(DgsDataFetchingEnvironment dfe) {
        DataLoader<Long, Author> dataLoader = dfe.getDataLoader("authorsLoader");
        Post post = dfe.getSource();
        return dataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());
    }

    @DgsData(parentType = "Post", field = "comments")
    public CompletableFuture<List<Comment>> comments(DgsDataFetchingEnvironment dfe) {
        DataLoader<Long, List<Comment>> dataLoader = dfe.getDataLoader(CommentsDataLoader.class);
        Post post = dfe.getSource();
        return dataLoader.load(post.getId());
    }

    @DgsMutation
    public Post createPost(@InputArgument("createPostInput") CreatePostInput input) {
        var id = this.postService.createPost(input);
        return this.postService.getPostById(id);
    }
}

The annotations, in order of appearance:

  • @DgsComponent — a Spring stereotype that marks the class as a container of data fetchers.
  • @DgsQuery / @DgsMutation — bind a method to a field on the Query / Mutation root type, matched by method name. allPosts() serves the allPosts field.
  • @DgsData(parentType = "Post", field = "author") — binds a method to a nested field on any type. dfe.getSource() returns the parent Post.
  • @InputArgument — binds a GraphQL argument to a parameter, coercing it to the parameter type. @InputArgument("createPostInput") names the argument explicitly because the parameter is input, not createPostInput.

The author and comments fetchers return CompletableFuture and go through a DataLoader; that is the N+1 fix we return to in the custom components section.

The GraphQL types themselves are plain Lombok value objects:

@Data
@Builder
public class Post {
    Long id;
    String title;
    String content;
    List<Comment> comments;
    Long authorId;
    Author author;
}

The input type carries Bean Validation constraints, which DGS enforces when you add @Valid to the argument (the dgs-webflux module does exactly that):

@Getter
@Setter
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class CreatePostInput {
    @NotEmpty
    @Length(min = 5, max = 100)
    String title;

    @NotEmpty
    String content;
}

A DataInitializer bean implements ApplicationRunner and seeds a handful of posts and comments on startup, so there is data to query immediately.

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
Start the shared PostgreSQL container from the repository root:

docker compose up -d postgres

The docker-compose.yml creates a blogdb database with user user and password password, which matches application.properties:

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost/blogdb
spring.datasource.username=user
spring.datasource.password=password
spring.sql.init.mode=always

Then run the application:

cd dgs
./mvnw spring-boot:run

On Windows use mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run. Once you see the "started DemoApplication" log line, open http://localhost:8080/graphiql.

docs.title: GraphiQL
docs.text:
DGS ships GraphiQL, an in-browser IDE that reads your schema through introspection and provides completion, documentation, and a query runner. On the left you browse the schema; on the right you run operations and read the response.

Create a post with the createPost mutation:

mutation {
  createPost(createPostInput: { title: "Hello DGS", content: "My first post" }) {
    id
    title
    content
  }
}

Then read it back. allPosts returns every post, resolving each author and comment list too:

{
  allPosts {
    id
    title
    content
    author { name email }
    comments { id content }
  }
}

And fetch one post by id with postById:

{
  postById(postId: "1") {
    id
    title
    content
    author { name email }
    comments { id content }
  }
}

Because the author and comments live in separate tables, allPosts is exactly where the DataLoaders earn their keep — a plain nested fetch would run one query per post.

docs.title: Switching to WebFlux
docs.text:
The dgs-webflux module runs the same blog domain on the reactive stack. The switch is mostly a dependency change:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-r2dbc</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
    <artifactId>r2dbc-postgresql</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

webmvc becomes webflux, and blocking JDBC becomes reactive R2DBC. The fetchers change their return types to Reactor types — the annotations stay the same:

@DgsComponent
@Validated
public class PostsDataFetcher {
    private final PostService postService;
    private final AuthorService authorService;

    @DgsQuery
    public Flux<Post> allPosts() {
        return this.postService.getAllPosts();
    }

    @DgsQuery
    public Mono<Post> postById(@InputArgument Long postId) {
        return this.postService.getPostById(postId);
    }

    @DgsMutation
    public Mono<Post> createPost(@InputArgument("createPostInput") @Valid CreatePostInput input) {
        return this.postService.createPost(input).flatMap(id -> this.postService.getPostById(id));
    }

    @DgsMutation
    public Mono<Comment> addComment(@InputArgument("commentInput") @Valid CommentInput input) {
        return this.postService.addComment(input);
    }

    @DgsSubscription
    Publisher<Comment> commentAdded() {
        return postService.commentAdded();
    }
}

Two things to notice:

  • @Valid on the argument turns on Bean Validation for CreatePostInput.
  • @DgsSubscription turns a method that returns a reactive Publisher into a live subscription — a stream of results pushed to the client, here over Server-Sent Events or WebSocket.

This module also adds a second mutation (addComment) and demonstrates the subscription transport, so it is the one to copy when you need real-time updates.

docs.title: Codegen for type safety
docs.text:
So far the types (Post, Author, CreatePostInput) are written by hand. The dgs-codegen module generates them from the schema with the DGS codegen plugin, so the Java types and the schema cannot drift apart. It also generates a DgsConstants class with the type and field names as constants.

The Maven setup wires the plugin in and adds the generated sources to the build:

<plugin>
    <groupId>io.github.deweyjose</groupId>
    <artifactId>graphqlcodegen-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <version>${dgs-codegen-plugin.version}</version>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>dgs-codegen</id>
            <goals><goal>generate</goal></goals>
            <configuration>
                <schemaPaths>
                    <param>${project.basedir}/src/main/resources/schema</param>
                </schemaPaths>
                <packageName>com.example.demo.gql</packageName>
                <generateClientApi>true</generateClientApi>
            </configuration>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

Because this is the Maven plugin rather than the Gradle one, you also add graphql-dgs-codegen-shared-core, which supplies the base classes of the generated client API.

With codegen, the schema is richer — it adds a PostStatus enum, a createdAt field, custom scalars, and a custom directive:

directive @uppercase on FIELD_DEFINITION
scalar LocalDateTime
scalar UUID

type Post {
    id: ID!
    title: String! @uppercase
    content: String
    comments: [Comment]
    status: PostStatus
    createdAt: LocalDateTime
    authorId: String
    author: Author
}

enum PostStatus {
    DRAFT, PENDING_MODERATION, PUBLISHED
}

The fetchers now reference the generated constants instead of hard-coded strings, and the generated types instead of hand-written ones:

@DgsData(
    parentType = DgsConstants.POST.TYPE_NAME,
    field = DgsConstants.POST.Author
)
public CompletableFuture<Author> author(DgsDataFetchingEnvironment dfe) {
    DataLoader<String, Author> dataLoader = dfe.getDataLoader("authorsLoader");
    Post post = dfe.getSource();
    return dataLoader.load(post.getAuthorId());
}

DgsConstants.POST.TYPE_NAME and DgsConstants.POST.Author are generated, so a schema rename becomes a compile error rather than a silent typo.

docs.title: Custom components
docs.text: DGS's extension points all follow the same pattern: implement an interface, annotate it with a @Dgs* annotation, and DGS registers it. This section covers the ones you will reach for most often.

docs.title: Custom scalars
docs.text:
A custom scalar teaches GraphQL Java how to serialize and parse a value type that is not one of the five built-in scalars. The dgs-codegen module declares scalar LocalDateTime and implements it with @DgsScalar:

@DgsScalar(name = "LocalDateTime")
public class LocalDateTimeScalar implements Coercing<LocalDateTime, String> {

    @Override
    public String serialize(Object dataFetcherResult, GraphQLContext ctx, Locale locale) {
        if (dataFetcherResult instanceof LocalDateTime dateTime) {
            return dateTime.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_DATE_TIME);
        }
        throw new CoercingSerializeException("Not a valid DateTime");
    }

    @Override
    public LocalDateTime parseLiteral(Value<?> input, CoercedVariables variables,
                                      GraphQLContext ctx, Locale locale) {
        if (input instanceof StringValue value) {
            return LocalDateTime.parse(value.getValue(), DateTimeFormatter.ISO_DATE_TIME);
        }
        throw new CoercingParseLiteralException("Value is not a valid ISO date time");
    }
}

serialize turns a LocalDateTime into the ISO string sent to the client; parseValue/parseLiteral do the reverse for input. A UUIDScalar does the same for java.util.UUID. The graphql-dgs-extended-scalars dependency ships ready-made scalars for common types if you would rather not write your own.

docs.title: Custom directives
docs.text:
A directive decorates a field and can change how it is fetched. The @uppercase directive wraps the field's data fetcher so the returned value is uppercased:

@DgsDirective(name = "uppercase")
public class UppercaseDirectiveWiring implements SchemaDirectiveWiring {

    @Override
    public GraphQLFieldDefinition onField(SchemaDirectiveWiringEnvironment<GraphQLFieldDefinition> env) {
        var field = env.getElement();
        var parentType = env.getFieldsContainer();
        var coordinates = FieldCoordinates.coordinates(parentType, field.getName());
        var original = env.getCodeRegistry().getDataFetcher(coordinates, field);

        var dataFetcher = DataFetcherFactories.wrapDataFetcher(original, (dfe, value) ->
                value instanceof String s ? s.toUpperCase() : value);

        env.getCodeRegistry().dataFetcher(coordinates, dataFetcher);
        return field;
    }
}

Because the schema marks title: String! @uppercase, every title that comes back from the server is upper-cased — the directive changed the field's behavior without touching the fetcher.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
When a data fetcher throws, DGS turns the exception into a GraphQL error. You can take over that mapping with a DataFetcherExceptionHandler and, using DGS's TypedGraphQLError, attach a well-known error type and HTTP-like status:

@Component
public class CustomDataFetchingExceptionHandler implements DataFetcherExceptionHandler {
    private final DefaultDataFetcherExceptionHandler defaultHandler =
            new DefaultDataFetcherExceptionHandler();

    @Override
    public CompletableFuture<DataFetcherExceptionHandlerResult> handleException(
            DataFetcherExceptionHandlerParameters handlerParameters) {
        Throwable exception = handlerParameters.getException();
        if (exception instanceof AuthorNotFoundException || exception instanceof PostNotFoundException) {
            GraphQLError error = TypedGraphQLError.newNotFoundBuilder()
                    .message(exception.getMessage())
                    .path(handlerParameters.getPath())
                    .build();
            return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(
                    DataFetcherExceptionHandlerResult.newResult().error(error).build());
        }
        return defaultHandler.handleException(handlerParameters);
    }
}

Now a postById for a missing id returns a typed NOT_FOUND error with a clear message instead of a generic stack trace. The dgs-webflux module goes one step further and also maps ConstraintViolationException to a typed BAD_REQUEST, so validation failures are reported consistently.

docs.title: Bean Validation
docs.text:
Input types are plain objects, so you validate them with the Jakarta Bean Validation annotations you already use in Spring MVC. Add constraints to the input class:

public class CreatePostInput {
    @NotEmpty
    @Length(min = 5, max = 100)
    String title;

    @NotEmpty
    String content;
}

Then mark the argument with @Valid (and the class with @Validated) as shown in the WebFlux section. A request with an empty title is rejected before it reaches your service.

docs.title: DataLoaders and the N+1 problem
docs.text:
A naive author fetcher would run one query per post — loading ten posts plus their authors means eleven queries. @DgsDataLoader batches and caches the lookups per request:

@DgsDataLoader(name = "authorsLoader")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class AuthorsDataLoader implements BatchLoader<Long, Author> {
    private final AuthorService authorService;

    @Override
    public CompletionStage<List<Author>> load(List<Long> keys) {
        return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> this.authorService.getAuthorByIdIn(keys));
    }
}

Instead of one query per id, the loader collects the keys during the execution tick and issues a single WHERE id IN (...) query. The fetcher looks the loader up by name and calls load(key) — the same pattern you saw in PostsDataFetcher. Use a loader for any nested field backed by a second table or a remote call.

docs.title: Typesafe client
docs.text:
The dgs-client module is a small command-line application that calls the GraphQL API with the client the codegen plugin generated. It is a separate module from the server: it declares the same schema, enables generateClientApi, and depends on graphql-dgs-client and spring-boot-starter-restclient.

The generated client API comes in two halves. A query object holds the operation, and a projection declares which fields you want:

GraphQLQueryRequest request = new GraphQLQueryRequest(
        new AllPostsGraphQLQuery(),
        new AllPostsProjectionRoot<AuthorProjection<?, ?>, PostProjection<?, ?>>()
                .id().title().content().status().parent()
                .author().id().name().email().parent()
                .comments().id().content().parent()
                .createdAt());

String query = request.serialize();

request.serialize() produces the GraphQL document. You then execute it with the DGS client, which rides Spring's RestClient:

DgsGraphQLClient client =
        new DgsRestClientGraphQLClient(RestClient.builder().baseUrl(url).build());

DgsGraphQLResponse response = client.executeQuery(query, Map.of());
List<Post> posts = response.extractValueAsObject("allPosts", new TypeRef<List<Post>>() {});

The projections are typesafe: you can only select fields that exist on the type, and extractValueAsObject deserializes into the generated Post. The module's test stubs the /graphql endpoint with WireMock and verifies the request body semantically, so the client is exercised without a running server.

docs.title: File upload
docs.text:
GraphQL does not define file uploads in the specification, and Spring GraphQL does not ship one. The dgs-fileupload module adds it back with the GraphQL multipart request specification via the multipart-spring-graphql library:

<dependency>
    <groupId>name.nkonev.multipart-spring-graphql</groupId>
    <artifactId>multipart-spring-graphql</artifactId>
    <version>${multipart-spring-graphql.version}</version>
</dependency>

The schema declares the Upload scalar and uses it in a mutation:

scalar Upload

type Mutation {
    upload(file: Upload!): Boolean
    uploadWithDesc(desc: String, file: Upload!): Boolean
    uploads(files: [Upload!]!): Boolean
}

In the data fetcher you read the file from the environment rather than via @InputArgument, because a MultipartFile cannot be deserialized through the Jackson object mapper:

@DgsComponent
public class FileUploadMutation {

    @DgsMutation
    public Boolean upload(DgsDataFetchingEnvironment env) {
        var file = (MultipartFile) env.getArgument("file");
        // read file.getInputStream(), file.getOriginalFilename(), file.getContentType()
        return true;
    }
}

The multipart parsing happens in the transport layer; your fetcher only sees the resolved MultipartFile.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
You now have a working DGS application and a tour of its extension points. The base dgs module shows the core programming model; dgs-webflux the reactive stack and subscriptions; dgs-codegen generated types, custom scalars, and directives; dgs-client the generated client; and dgs-fileupload multipart uploads.

From here:

  • Read the DGS documentation for federation, testing, and the full annotation reference.
  • Look at the dgs-kotlin and dgs-kotlin-co modules for the same domain in Kotlin and coroutines.
  • See DGS or Spring GraphQL? for how DGS relates to the Spring team's framework.
